verdicts.strongest_argument: The two treasury endpoints check out exactly against the primary notices — 3,993,501 after the 26-29 May purchase and 4,699,397 after the 24-28 Aug purchase, a delta of 705,896 shares over 13 weeks, ~54k/week, and shares outstanding 409,803,623 — so the aggregation is not fabricated. But two of the three things the hunter builds on top of that arithmetic do not survive the primary record. First, 'decaying monotonically' is refuted by the hunter's own cited URL: detail/157 reports 47,000 shares for 31 Aug-4 Sep, after 17k, 13k and 23k, i.e. the pace has tripled off its trough in the last three weeks and the most recent week is at the 13-week average, not below it. Second, '~85%' is a peak-week-to-trough-week comparison dressed as a run-rate. On like-for-like verified endpoints the step-down is much smaller and it is a step, not a decay: 3,018,501 (2 Apr) → 3,708,501 (1 May) is 690,000 shares in ~4.2 weeks (164k/wk); 3,708,501 → 3,993,501 (29 May) is 285,000 (71k/wk); then 54k/wk for the next 13 weeks. So the whole break happens in the single week the company closed the $650m Reliant/Aries acquisition (1 May 2026) and it has been roughly flat since — May to August is -24%, not -85%. The 85% figure only exists against the FY26 total of $1,413m, which is not a run-rate: that number is dominated by the tail of the FIRST $1.5bn programme, an explicit 18-month completion sprint that ended 24 Feb 2026, and the company disclosed it as such on 23 June. Third, the cause is guided. On 23 June management disclosed the Reliant close, raised FY27 net rental capex to $2.05-2.45bn (an International Rental News headline that day was literally 'Sunbelt makes $650m acquisition and ups 2027 CapEx'), reported net leverage 1.6x, and ranked capital allocation as organic first, bolt-on M&A second, dividend and buyback last. A company that has just spent $650m of cash and raised capex buying back less is the disclosed plan executing, not a signal. On publication: each weekly notice is an RNS-format wire release syndicated same-day by TipRanks, Yahoo UK Finance, MarketScreener, Stockopedia and Reuters, with the treasury count and shares outstanding in the body — the inputs are ubiquitous. The hunter is right that nobody assembles them into a series (TipRanks' 1 Sep write-up of the same notice offers no pace commentary at all), which is what keeps this out of the 80s. On materiality: 54k shares/week against 6.1m ADV is under 0.2% of a single day's volume, so there is no flow-support channel; the foregone ~$1.2bn/yr of repurchase is ~4.3% of a $27.7bn cap in annual flow but only ~1.5-2% of shares per year, i.e. ~1-2% on out-year EPS, and it is spread over years rather than landing in tomorrow's print. The one live channel is the call — management said the Q1 quarterly dividend would be announced with Q1 results — but that cuts both ways: a dividend-for-buyback reallocation is the most likely reading and it is not bearish.

prior_publication.what_it_says: The hunter's own source: 47,000 shares bought 31 Aug-4 Sep at $65.71-$71.95, the largest week since early July, which breaks the 'monotonically decaying' element of the claim.
Syndicated write-up of the 24-28 Aug notice giving treasury 4,699,397 and shares outstanding 409,803,623 — the exact endpoint the aggregation rests on, on the wire a week before the hunter used it.
30 Mar-2 Apr week: 330,000 shares, treasury 3,018,501, shares in issue 410,945,584 — the early-programme anchor that shows the true step-down is ~65-70% from programme start, not 85%.
Reuters/RNS carry of the 27 Apr-1 May notice: 75,000 shares at $73.66-$77.10, treasury 3,708,501, shares in issue 410,255,584.

Company Q4 FY26 release states the first $1.5bn programme completed 24 Feb 2026 and the second commenced 2 Mar 2026, FY26 buybacks $1,413m and dividends $464m, net leverage 1.6x, Reliant $650m, and FY27 net rental capex $2.05-2.45bn — i.e. the cash reallocation that explains the step-down was disclosed.
Trade-press headline on the same day framing the quarter as a $650m acquisition plus a capex raise, the two uses of cash that displaced buyback.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The tape gives the claim no support. The 20-day run-up of -14.35% starts around 10 Aug, weeks after the buyback pace had already settled at its lower level (the break was the week of 1 May), so the drawdown does not line up with the slowdown; more plausible coincident causes are the sector derate and the 4 Sep S&P 500 rebalance in which SUNB was not among the additions. Options run the wrong way for a bearish capital-return story: 25d skew -3.35 vol points (calls bid over puts) and put/call open interest 0.02 on 16,845 contracts — essentially nobody is paying for downside. I put almost no weight on the 2-event history (both down, -9.41% and -1.94%), and the 46%-of-mid ATM spread means the 9.76% implied move is indicative only.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: If tomorrow's release or 10-Q shows the programme formally suspended, downsized, or the remaining authorisation cancelled — rather than simply under-spent while Reliant and capex absorbed cash — this becomes a real capital-allocation event and drops toward 25.

verdicts.strongest_argument: Every component of this is in the wire copy, and most of it is in the company's own guidance. The Reliant/Aries $650m close on 1 May 2026 was announced in the 23 June Q4 press release and carried by Businesswire, Morningstar, Yahoo and the rental trade press the same morning; FY27 guidance of 5-8% rental revenue growth and $4.85-5.05bn adjusted EBITDA already contains it, so the 'inorganic boost' is definitionally in consensus rather than incremental to it. The ~$70m of FIFA World Cup and UFC event revenue was volunteered by management on the 23 June call and is in the transcript the hunter is citing — a number management itself labelled one-time, which is the opposite of an unpriced upside: sell-side has it in the Q1 bridge and will strip it out. 'Margins improve in the back half' is management's own words and is bearish for Q1 optics, not bullish; the market's reaction to that same guidance was -9.41% on the day. The peer data is the most-covered news in the sector this summer: United Rentals reported record Q2 and raised FY26 revenue guidance to $17.5-17.8bn from $16.9-17.4bn on 22 July, on rental revenue +12.7% and fleet productivity +3.4%, and Herc raised 2026 equipment rental revenue guidance to $4.375-4.475bn on Q2 revenue +20% — both were Reuters/Nasdaq/Globe and Mail headlines that repriced the whole group. The residual, genuinely-unpublished piece is only the inference: that the easy +2.4% Q1 FY26 comp plus a Q4 exit rate of +8.0% plus peer strength means Q1 volumes beat. But the options already express exactly that inference — negative 25d skew and a put/call OI ratio of 0.02 say the market is paying for upside into this print, not hedging it. A bullish finding on a name where the only thing anyone owns is calls is agreement, not information. The one honest deduction is that SUNB fell 14.35% over 20 days while the peers were raising, so the market has plainly declined to extrapolate — but the readier explanations for that gap are Sunbelt-specific margin scepticism (the same worry that produced the June drop, and the reason three analysts cut fair value to $78 from $83.64) and index flow around the FTSE exit and the 4 Sep S&P 500 rebalance that passed SUNB over.

prior_publication.what_it_says: Q4 FY26 results: Reliant Asset Management (Aries Building Systems) closed 1 May 2026 for $650m, FY27 guidance of 4.5-7.5% total and 5-8% rental revenue growth, adjusted EBITDA $4.85-5.05bn, net rental capex $2.05-2.45bn.
The call transcript the finding cites: management quantifies ~$70m of one-time non-construction event revenue around FIFA/World Cup landing in Q1 FY27 and says margins improve in the back half.
URI record Q2: rental revenue +12.7% to $3.849bn, fleet productivity +3.4%, FY26 revenue guidance raised to $17.5-17.8bn and adjusted EBITDA to $7.975-8.125bn.
Herc Q2 revenue +20% to $1.204bn, adjusted EBITDA +19% to $487m, 2026 equipment rental revenue guidance raised to $4.375-4.475bn.
Trade coverage of the same release confirming the Reliant/Aries modular acquisition and the Specialty strategy framing on the day it was announced.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Options are the strongest evidence against novelty here: 25d skew -3.35 vol points (put IV below call IV, unusual into an event) and a put/call open interest ratio of 0.02 on 16,845 contracts, which the baseline itself labels 'upside paid'. That is the bullish thesis already expressed in positioning. Against that, the 20-day run-up of -14.35% and -21.52% from the 52-week high say the underlying has derated through the peer-beat window, which is the only part of the finding that has any claim to being unpriced. The 2-event history is too thin to weigh, and the 46%-of-mid ATM spread means the 9.76% implied move should not be read precisely; I treat the skew sign as the usable signal and the level as noise.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: If consensus Q1 rental revenue growth can be shown to sit near the +2.4% comp rather than near the +5-8% FY27 guide plus Reliant — i.e. the sell-side has not actually put the guided inorganic and event revenue into the Q1 line — this drops toward 45.

interactions: The two findings rest on the same document and are two readings of the same decision. Both trace to the 23 June 2026 Q4 FY26 release and call: SUNB#1 explicitly (the ~$70m event revenue, 'margins improve in the back half', the Reliant close), SUNB#0 implicitly (the $1,413m FY26 buyback total, the 1.6x leverage, the $650m Reliant cash outflow and the raised FY27 capex). They also point opposite ways from one cause. SUNB#0 reads the post-1-May buyback step-down as an ominous throttle; SUNB#1 counts the Reliant acquisition that closed on exactly 1 May as an inorganic revenue tailwind. It is the same $650m. Whatever weight the ranking gives to Reliant boosting Q1 revenue it must also give to Reliant, not caution, being why the buyback stepped down that week — they cannot both be scored as independent surprises. Practically, SUNB#0's verified May-29 and Aug-28 treasury endpoints are correct and I concede that no vendor turns the weekly notices into a series; what fails is the 85% magnitude and the 'monotonic decay' shape, the latter refuted by the hunter's own cited URL (47,000 shares in the 31 Aug-4 Sep week, up from a 13,000 trough).
